assessment: The incumbent combines a predictable conversational routine with printed preparation and optional messaging. Seven frequent attendees explicitly value its repetition, and print serves nine regular print-only users. Familiarity may reduce entry effort for regulars, but that causal account is untested. H3-O6 supplies a concrete limit: five occasional attendees struggled to enter conversations familiar to partners. Pair delays and switches are consistent with entry friction but do not establish its cause. Useful-practice reports were 49/72 and correct preparation identification 48/72; neither establishes the targets across all 97 attendances. Coordination sometimes exceeded 90 minutes. Untimed practice, blanks, and unlinked slips limit attribution.

openings.claim: Unequal familiarity with conversational context may impede entry independently of proficiency.
openings.delta: Retain the repeated routine but test a self-contained first prompt supplying both partners the same starting context, without public proficiency labels or prior-attendance requirements.
openings.prediction: Relative to existing prompts, shared-context prompts reduce time to both partners' first substantive contribution and early partner switching, especially where prior familiarity differs.
openings.probe: Across six sessions, alternate comparable existing and shared-context prompts between pair groups. Observe entry latency, switches, and individual speaking duration; collect anonymous useful-practice reports and optional private familiarity responses. Keep practice inside 75 minutes and record added volunteer effort.
assumptions: Comparable prompts can be prepared within the coordination budget.
Observation can distinguish context-entry friction from unequal speaking turns; neither cause is established.

openings.claim: Preparation errors may partly reflect ambiguity about which week a task belongs to.
openings.delta: Test a paper calendar of six dated preparation tasks, reissued at attendance, with the next date visibly marked and each task usable after missed sessions.
openings.prediction: Earlier-task substitutions decrease; unchanged errors despite correct date recognition would weaken temporal ambiguity as the explanation.
openings.probe: Ask anonymous exit respondents separately for the next session date and preparation task. Compare error types with baseline, retain blanks in the denominator, record print-only responses, and log weekly coordination minutes including calendar preparation.
assumptions: Volunteers can select six conversational topics in advance within the weekly time target.
Advance paper copies remain usable during absences; attendance never depends on preparation.
